meta.title: Turkish A2
meta.subtitle: 600 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Turkish → English (see the Turkish, recall the meaning) and English → Turkish (see an English meaning, recall the Turkish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 600 words for level A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: the Yunus Emre Institute's Turkish Proficiency Exam (TYS) certifies only B2 and C1 and publishes no vocabulary list. The scope of this deck is taken instead from the Turkish as a Foreign Language Teaching Programme (Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı; Türkiye Maarif Foundation, 2nd edition, 2020, approved by Turkey's Ministry of National Education), a CEFR-based syllabus whose A2 tables for secondary school (pp. 255–264) are organised in ten themes: coming back from a holiday, weekend plans, a daily routine, the news, careers and the family, living together by rules, technology, sport and healthy eating, telling a story, and travel. FROM A2 UP THE PROGRAMME LISTS NO VOCABULARY AT ALL: its A2 table says the vocabulary section was left out so as not to limit the level. What each theme gives instead is its suggested topics — holiday memories, clubs, cinema and concerts, timetables, the news and the weather, professions and the extended family, rules at school and on the road, phones and computers, sports and food, fables and their animals, feelings, transport, tourism and camping. So 260 of the 600 words were written for Folio for those topics, a theme at a time, and are Folio's choice rather than the programme's; 17 more are words its A2 grammar list itself names (aynı, zorunda, lazım, birkaç, hepsi …). This is not an official word list and is not presented as one. No word taught in the levels below is repeated. The other 323 are the commonest words of everyday Turkish, from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles. The cards are ordered by that frequency, so the words met most often come first; the one two-word expression, which a list of single words cannot count, comes last. Turkish builds words by adding suffixes, and a suffix's vowel follows the vowels of the word (vowel harmony) while some stems change before it, so the card carries the forms that cannot be guessed, read from a dictionary rather than generated. 292 nouns show their plural and five cases — şekil: şekiller, şekli, şekle, şekilde, şekilden, şeklin. 102 verbs show the third person of the present, the aorist (the general present), the past and the future — dilemek: diliyor, diler, diledi, dileyecek — the aorist's vowel being the one a learner cannot predict. 2 pronouns show their cases. Adjectives do not inflect and carry no forms. Real example sentences come with 599 of the 600 words, three apiece for 597, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Scope: Türkçenin Yabancı Dil Olarak Öğretimi Programı, Türkiye Maarif Vakfı, 2020 (ISBN 978-605-80438-2-4). Meanings, forms and parts of speech: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency ordering: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
